early_history_summary: Born in Lorette, Loire, Prost discovered karting at age 14 during a family trip to Monaco. He won the French junior karting championship and the Winfield racing school competition, which earned him a place in Formula Renault. He dominated junior categories, winning the European Formula 3 Championship in 1979, and signed for McLaren's F1 team in 1980.
family_context_summary: Born to a French father who manufactured kitchen furnishings and an Armenian mother. His father owned a store where Prost worked to save money for his first go-kart. The family was middle-class, and his father supported his racing ambitions, taking him to the Monaco Grand Prix at age 15.
parent_family_domain_summary: His father was a small business owner (kitchen furnishings manufacturer) who provided financial support and encouragement for Prost's racing career. By 24, he had won the European Formula 3 Championship, and by 26 he had his first F1 victory.

milestone_by_age_26: Won the WWF Intercontinental Championship on February 13, 1997 at age 24, defeating Hunter Hearst Helmsley on Monday Night Raw, months after his WWF debut at Survivor Series in November 1996.
early_history_summary: Johnson grew up in a wrestling family—his father Rocky Johnson was a WWE Tag Team Champion and his maternal grandfather Peter Maivia was also a professional wrestler. After a failed football career (University of Miami backup, undrafted by NFL, cut by Calgary Stampeders), his father helped him secure a WWF contract in 1996. He wrestled briefly as Flex Kavana in the USWA, winning tag team titles, then debuted on WWF TV as Rocky Maivia at Survivor Series 1996. Within three months he won the Intercontinental Championship at age 24.
family_context_summary: Son of Rocky Johnson (born Wayde Douglas Bowles), a Black Nova Scotian professional wrestler, and Ata Fitisemanu (née Maivia), of Samoan descent. His father and Tony Atlas were the first black tag team champions in WWE history. His maternal grandfather Peter Maivia was also a professional wrestler, and his maternal grandmother Lia was one of the first female pro wrestling promoters.
parent_family_domain_summary: Deep multi-generational wrestling lineage: father Rocky Johnson was a WWE wrestler, maternal grandfather Peter Maivia was a wrestler, maternal grandmother was a wrestling promoter, and through Maivia he is connected to the Anoaʻi wrestling family. His father directly helped him secure a WWF contract in 1996.
primary_early_advantage_tags: wrestling family dynasty, father's WWF contract help, grandfather Peter Maivia, Anoaʻi family, third-generation wrestler, WWF Attitude Era
evidence_summary: Johnson's rapid rise to Intercontinental Champion at 24 was overwhelmingly enabled by his multi-generational wrestling family. His father Rocky Johnson (WWE Tag Team Champion) directly helped secure his WWF contract, his grandfather Peter Maivia was a wrestling legend, and his maternal grandmother was a pioneering female wrestling promoter. The WWF hyped him as their first third-generation wrestler. His football background provided athletic foundation, but the wrestling family network was the decisive advantage. The emerging Attitude Era provided a structural wave of growing wrestling popularity.

name: Ronaldinho
milestone_by_age_26: Won the 2002 FIFA World Cup with Brazil at age 22, scoring two goals including a famous free kick against England; subsequently won FIFA World Player of the Year in 2004 (age 24) and 2005 (age 25), and the 2005 Ballon d'Or.
early_history_summary: Ronaldinho joined the Grêmio youth academy at age seven in 1987 and spent eleven years there before making his professional debut in 1998 at age 18. He won the FIFA Under-17 World Championship in 1997 as tournament best player, debuted for the Brazilian senior national team in 1999 winning the Copa América, and was an integral part of the 2002 World Cup winning team. He moved to Paris Saint-Germain in 2001 and then Barcelona in 2003, where he won his first FIFA World Player of the Year award.
family_context_summary: Ronaldinho was born to a working-class family in Porto Alegre, Brazil. His father João was a shipyard worker and amateur footballer, and his mother Miguelina was a salesperson. His older brother Roberto signed with Grêmio, which gave the family a villa. His father tragically drowned in the family pool when Ronaldinho was eight years old.
parent_family_domain_summary: Ronaldinho's father João was an amateur footballer for a local club and worked as a shipyard worker; his older brother Roberto was a promising professional player at Grêmio. The family was deeply immersed in football, with uncles and father all playing, providing direct domain exposure from birth.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Grêmio academy, Brazilian football culture, father and brother footballers, physical prodigy, World Cup at 22
evidence_summary: Ronaldinho grew up in a working-class family in Porto Alegre deeply immersed in football — his father was an amateur player and his brother Roberto signed professionally with Grêmio, which gave the family a home. He joined Grêmio's youth academy at age seven and spent eleven years there, developing extraordinary skills recognized when he scored 23 goals in a single game at age 13. He won the FIFA U-17 World Championship in 1997 as best player, debuted professionally in 1998, and was a key part of Brazil's 2002 World Cup winning team at age 22. His father's death when he was eight created hardship but also deepened his determination. Brazil's football culture and the Grêmio academy pipeline were critical early advantages.

name: Vitali Klitschko
milestone_by_age_26: Won silver at the 1995 World Amateur Boxing Championships in Berlin and gold at the 1995 Military World Games in Ariccia, Italy, at age 24; was also a six-time kickboxing world champion (amateur and professional) by age 25, with an amateur boxing record of 195-15.
early_history_summary: Vitali Klitschko began boxing at age 17 in 1988, trained by Anatoliy Klimanov at the CSKA Kyiv Sports Club. He competed simultaneously in amateur boxing, kickboxing, and sport karate, achieving considerable success in all three. By 1994-1995 he was winning medals at the World Championships and Military World Games, and was a six-time kickboxing world champion before turning professional in 1996.
family_context_summary: Klitschko's father Volodymyr was a Soviet Air Force major general and military attaché, and his mother Nadiya was a teacher. The family lived in various Soviet locations including Czechoslovakia and Pripyat (near Chernobyl). His father was a Chernobyl cleanup commander who later died of cancer. The military background provided discipline and access to Soviet sports infrastructure.
parent_family_domain_summary: Klitschko's father was a career military officer, not directly involved in sports, but the Soviet military system provided access to elite sports training facilities and the CSKA Kyiv Sports Club pipeline. The family's military background instilled discipline and provided educational opportunities.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Soviet sports system, CSKA Kyiv, Klimanov coaching, brother Wladimir, military family discipline, physical specimen
evidence_summary: Vitali Klitschko grew up in a Soviet military family — his father was an Air Force major general — which provided access to the Soviet sports infrastructure and disciplined training environment. He began boxing at 17 under Anatoliy Klimanov, a 1974 World Championships bronze medalist, at the CSKA Kyiv Sports Club. His younger brother Wladimir was also an elite boxer, creating a high-trust training partnership. Klitschko's exceptional physical stature (6'7", powerful hitter) and the Soviet military sports pipeline enabled rapid development, leading to World Championship silver and Military World Games gold by age 24, plus six kickboxing world titles. The family's displacement from Pripyat after Chernobyl added adversity.
